name: Lacrosse ball / massage gun
lead: A lacrosse ball is a firm rubber ball used for self-massage against a wall or floor, and a massage gun is a handheld battery-powered percussive device that delivers rapid pulses, commonly 20 to 60 Hz, through interchangeable heads. Both are used for muscle tension, soreness and trigger-point release.[1]

Research on percussive massage is described as limited. Randomized and crossover studies have examined recovery, range of motion and pain, and a case report documented rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use.[2][3][4] On looksmax.org, users also discuss massage guns in connection with bonesmashing, a practice with no published support.[5][6]

paras: Electric percussive massagers were patented in the mid-twentieth century and sold mostly to physiotherapists and chiropractors until the 2010s. Consumer models spread after Theragun, developed by chiropractor Jason Wersland, and Hyperice's Hypervolt in 2018, with social media and the COVID-19 period boosting sales.[1]

A 5-minute massage gun application was tested for perceptual and physical recovery in active adults, in a study whose authors called the devices new and under-researched.[2] A trial examined percussive massage with and without heat on calf muscle properties.[7] A self-myofascial release study of the superficial back line reported improved sit-and-reach distance.[8] A randomized trial tested local vibration therapy in cervical disc herniation for pain and function.[9] A case report described using a lacrosse ball with compression tack and flossing for adolescent Achilles tendinopathy.[10] No studies found testing either tool for facial structure or bone changes.
A 2021 case report in Physical Therapy described rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use.[3] Forum users note the heads could harm the eye area at high settings.[6]
Users on looksmax.org ask whether bonesmashing combined with a massage gun has any effect, and some say the soft attachments are unlikely to change bone but may help asymmetry.[5][6]

timeline.event: US patent for an electric percussive massager.[1]

lore.intro: Massage guns appear in looksmaxxing threads mainly alongside bonesmashing and muscle-tension discussions.[5][6]

claims.claim: A massage gun can reduce facial asymmetry
claims.believers: One forum poster says using a massage gun could decrease the chance of asymmetries, while stating the soft heads would not create new bone.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined massage guns for facial asymmetry.

claims.claim: Bonesmashing with a massage gun changes facial bones
claims.believers: Users ask whether the combination works, noting few answers in the forum.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this; the studies found examine muscle recovery, not bone remodelling.[2]

card.summary: Self-massage tools for muscle tension; research is limited to recovery and mobility, with nothing on looks.
card.aka: Percussive massager, Theragun-style, trigger point ball
card.note: A rhabdomyolysis case report exists; bonesmashing use is untested.

quick.overview:
A lacrosse ball is pressed against a wall or floor for self-massage, while a massage gun hammers tissue with fast pulses. Both target muscle knots and soreness.

Studies cover recovery and mobility. Nothing has tested them for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Pressure or percussion on soft tissue, intended to ease tension, aid range of motion and reduce soreness.[1][2]
quick.risks: A case report links massage gun use to rhabdomyolysis.[3] Regulatory status is that of a consumer wellness device.
